newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSSIE RULES-Best on Ground - Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules column.
newsitem.headline: AUSSIE RULES-Best on Ground - Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules column.

text.p: *By Andrew Bartram
TESTING TIME FOR TRIBUNAL
The AFL tribunal has been roundly criticised this year for perceived inconsistencies regarding verdicts and penalties.
It copped a head-high tackle from some sections of the Melbourne media for its handling of a case involving Sydney's Tony Lockett and Melbourne's Shaun Smith in Round 18.

The giant full-forward, who is no stranger to the tribunal having appeared 14 times, copped a two match penalty for charging the Demon defender rendering him unconscious and temporarily numb down one side.
It was suggested Lockett escaped lightly and if two weeks was his penalty other players with clean records should escape conviction.
Such inconsistencies have led to calls for mandatory penalties for specific offences such as two weeks for striking and tripping and one week for charging.
This week Geelong captain Barry Stoneham was caught by the video police and brought before the tribunal following an incident in which Essendon's Michael Symons received a broken jaw.
Stoneham, whose team will play in the finals was suspended until the end of the home and away series.

The previous week the tribunal found Carlton's Luke O'Sullivan guilty of breaking Adelaide's Trent Ormond-Allen's jaw and suspended him four weeks or, coincidentally, until the end of the home and away series.
Early last month St Kilda's Barry Hall was suspended by the tribunal for five weeks after he broke the jaw of a North Melbourne opponent in a reserves game.

Three similar incidents with the same result but different penalties. Why? Where is the consistency from the tribunal and what role, if any, does the finals play in determining sentences, even verdicts.
THE MCINTYRE SYSTEM
If you thought it was difficult deciding which teams would make the final-eight, try nutting out the workings of the McIntyre Final eight System.
With help from the Football Record Finals edition, Best On Ground will try to explain how the final eight works.
In the first week, the qualifying finals, the top side plays eighth, second plays seventh, third plays sixth and fourth plays fifth.

After the first week of the finals fixtures for the next two weeks are determined by ranking all eight teams depending on the result of their qualifying final and where they finished after the home and away season.

After the qualifying finals the two lowest ranked losers are eliminated while the highest ranked winners win a bye and progress to the third week. Obviously the advantage goes with the teams finishing the home and away series in the top two ladder positions.

In the second week, the semi finals, each match becomes sudden death. The number three ranked winner plays the number one ranked loser in the second semi-final while in the first semi-final, the number four ranked winner plays the number two ranked loser.
In week three four teams remain to contest the preliminary finals for the right to play in the grand final.
The winner of the second semi-final plays the number two ranked winner while the first semi-final winner plays the number one ranker winner.
The grand final pits the winners of both preliminary finals against each other.
In the event of a tie in any of the minor finals, overtime is played, except in the grand final which is replayed the following week.

Confused? Don't be discouraged. As its inventor Ken McIntyre told the Football Record: "Just make sure your team keeps winning and read about who and where they'll be playing in the papers on Monday".
THE TALE OF LEWIS AND THE CHEER SQUAD

The Hawthorn Football Club cheer squad caused a minor stir during the week when it lodged a formal complaint with the AFL alleging West Coast star Chris Lewis bared his backside to squad members during last week's game at Waverley Park.
The complaint was made directly to the League and without the knowledge and consent of the Hawthorn Football Club which, to say the least, was a little browned off with the squad.
The alleged incident completed an indifferent game for Lewis who fractured his arm in the Eagles' comfortable win.
He'll be forced to watch from the WACA sidelines tonight as his team demolishes Melbourne.

In matches tomorrow, Essendon will beat Collingwood at the MCG, St Kilda will do likewise to Fremantle at Waverley Park, Geelong will rebound against Carlton at Kardinia Park and Brisbane will make it three losses on the trot for Port Adelaide when they meet at the Gabba.
On Sunday, Sydney will thrash Hawthorn at the SCG, North Melbourne will kill Richmond at the MCG and Adelaide will be too strong for Western Bulldogs at Football Park.
*Andrew Bartram will be writing a regular AFL column for Reuters.
